edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice 3rd ed., Security tactics (Resist Attacks)
edges.note: Authorize Actors grants rights to an already-authenticated actor; its definition presupposes authentication.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Security tactics (Resist Attacks)
edges.note: Authentication verifies the claimed identity of an actor first identified as the source of input.
Nonrepudiation rests on digital signatures, which use the same asymmetric cryptography as encryption.
Nonrepudiation binds a message to an identity via certificates / trusted-third-party authentication.
A digital signature signs a message hash, so nonrepudiation depends on message-integrity verification.
An audit trail of signed actions provides the retained evidence that supports nonrepudiation claims.
Audit records timestamp each action so the sequence and timing of events can be reconstructed.
Audit logs of requests are the data that signature-based intrusion detection and forensics analyze.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Encrypt Data tactic
edges.note: Encryption provides confidentiality beyond authorization controls; the two layer to protect data.

edges.cite: Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns — Secure Channel
edges.note: A Secure Channel encrypts communication in transit, directly realizing the encrypt-data tactic on links.

edges.cite: Schumacher et al., Security Patterns — Secure Channel
edges.note: Secure Channel authenticates its endpoints before establishing the encrypted session.
SSO centralizes and reuses a single authentication act across multiple services.
Zero trust layers continuous verification at every boundary — a defense-in-depth strategy.
Zero trust continuously (re)authenticates every actor rather than trusting network location.
Zero trust enforces per-request, least-privilege authorization at each boundary.
The Authorization security pattern is a concrete realization of the authorize-actors tactic.
PDP/PEP splits and realizes the access-decision mechanism of the authorize-actors tactic.
A valet key grants scoped, time-limited authorization to a single resource — a narrowed authorization.
Federated identity relies on a trusted identity provider to authenticate actors across domains.
Cross-organization SSO is commonly built on federated-identity trust between providers.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Limit Access tactic
edges.note: A firewall is a concrete mechanism that limits access points and permitted traffic types.

edges.cite: Schumacher et al., Security Patterns — Packet Filter / Proxy-Based Firewall patterns
edges.note: Proxy-Based Firewall is a firewall pattern variant that filters at the application layer.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Limit Access tactic
edges.note: A DMZ is the canonical realization of limit-access, restricting reachable resources between zones.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Limit Access tactic
edges.note: A DMZ is bounded by a pair of firewalls separating internet, DMZ, and intranet.
A sandbox confines untrusted code, restricting the resources and interfaces it may access.
A Gatekeeper node validates and sanitizes requests before forwarding them to protected hosts.
A Gatekeeper brokers all traffic through one hardened node, reducing the reachable attack surface.
An IDS is the pattern that realizes the signature-based detect-intrusion tactic.
Limiting access points and limiting what each point exposes are complementary resist tactics.
Separating entities compartmentalizes value, reducing what any single breach can expose.
Compartmentalizing so no single point holds much value is a core defense-in-depth measure.
Physical/virtual separation adds an independent layer that a single compromise cannot cross.
Both isolate components onto separate resources to contain the blast radius of a failure/attack.
A TEE isolates sensitive code/data in a hardware-protected enclave, separated from the normal world.
Splitting a program into least-privileged parts limits what compromise of any one part can reach.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., availability/safety tactics (Masking)
edges.note: Masking resolves divergent redundant results through a voting procedure.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., availability/safety tactics (Masking)
edges.note: Masking compares the results of several redundant components before voting.
TMR masks a faulty result by majority vote over three redundant channels.
A MooN voting architecture (IEC 61508 notation) is the redundancy-architecture realization of voting.
MooN voting masks faulty channels by majority so a faulty output never propagates.
Lockstep runs two cores on identical input and compares outputs each cycle to detect faults.
Comparison flags divergence among redundant outputs; voting resolves it into a single value.
Both are failure-detection tactics; comparison uses redundancy, sanity-checking uses plausibility rules.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Safety tactics (limit consequences)
edges.note: Both limit the consequences of an unsafe state: abort terminates, degradation drops functionality.
On a detected fault one can either fail safe by aborting or mask the fault and continue.
An interlock barrier can trigger a fail-safe abort when an illegal sequence is attempted.
Both recover from a bad state: repair-state corrects it forward, rollback reverts to a good checkpoint.
Repair-state enlarges the set of states a component handles competently — the increase-competence-set idea.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Substitution safety tactic (after Wu & Kelly)
edges.note: Substitution replaces hazardous software with hardware protections such as interlocks.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Substitution safety tactic (after Wu & Kelly)
edges.note: Substitution replaces hazardous software with hardware devices such as watchdogs.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 3rd ed., Substitution safety tactic (after Wu & Kelly)
edges.note: Substitution employs hardware monitors that provide and control their own resources.
A Safety Executive coordinates safety mechanisms including interlocks that enforce safe sequencing.
Login lockout after repeated failures protects the authentication mechanism against brute force.
Both react-to-attack by restricting access; lockout is automatic/targeted, revoke is broad/emergency.
Forcing default-credential changes and periodic rotation strengthens the authentication tactic.
A secrets-management service automates the credential rotation this tactic requires.
A secrets manager encrypts stored credentials and keys at rest, realizing encrypt-data for secrets.
When intrusion is detected, inform-actors notifies operators/systems to react.
Detecting a DoS pattern feeds admission-control throttling as the mitigating reaction.
A detected denial-of-service triggers notification of operators for response.
Both counter man-in-the-middle attacks: one checks timing anomalies, the other message tampering.
Detecting delivery-time anomalies relies on timestamps to measure delivery latency.
Integrity (hash/MAC) and confidentiality (encryption) are combined, e.g. in authenticated encryption.
React tactics: on suspected attack, revoke access and notify relevant actors together.
Access is revoked in reaction to an intrusion the detection tactic surfaces.
Identifying the source of each input lets the audit trail attribute recorded actions to actors.
Both inspect incoming input for malicious content — validation blocks it, detection flags patterns.
